units.source_en: ### “Fire, Fire, Fire!”

paragraphs.source_en: A fire on a submarine was one of the most life-threatening accidents we could have. Not only would thick black smoke force us to wear our emergency air breathing (EAB) devices; the visibility would be reduced to near zero. Unchecked, the fire would grow in size, and the contained atmosphere in the boat would result in heat and pressure increases that would make human existence impossible. Eleven years previously, in April 1988, a fire aboard the USS *Bonefish* killed three sailors. In that fire, the heat got so intense that the shoes of crew members standing on the deck above the fire melted.

paragraphs.source_en: I was standing just forward of the crew’s mess, which was full of nukes in training, when the fire alarm rang. The department heads ran the drill programs but I approved all the drills, including when and how they would start. The engineer had briefed the drill monitors that the fire would be in the storeroom just aft of the crew’s mess. I wanted to see what would happen because I had been previously frustrated that it took too long to get immediate extinguishing agents and fire hoses to the fire.
